name: Naturalistic fallacy fallacy
statement: Searle named the naturalistic fallacy fallacy: treating every move from is to ought as a mistake, so that naming the fallacy is taken to settle the question.
meaning: This is the counter-charge, and it has two forms which are worth keeping apart. The first is procedural. A speaker meets an argument by naming a fallacy, and the name is treated as the refutation, although whether the argument commits it is the thing in dispute. The second is substantive. A speaker treats any passage from factual premises to a normative conclusion as an instance of the error, so that a valid derivation and a careless slide are given the same verdict. Four neighbouring entries hold the ground this one borders. Entry 432 covers what Moore actually charged, which is a claim about defining 'good' rather than about inference, and it records Frankena's objection that the charge cannot be assumed at the outset to mark a mistake of any kind. Entry 435 covers Hume's paragraph and Searle's five-step derivation from a promise to an obligation. Entry 434 covers the everyday preference for what is natural, which is a measured preference and not an argument. Entry 517 covers the move in the other direction, from ought to is. Entry 513 covers the general shape, the argument from fallacy, of which this is one label's worth. The general version and this one differ in what is at stake. The general version concerns whether a conclusion survives a bad argument for it. This one concerns the prior question, whether the argument is faulty at all, which is where the naturalistic fallacy and the is-ought thesis have been contested since 1939.

origin.note: The phrase occurs once in the paper that derives an 'ought' from an 'is', at page 48, and Searle does not define it. He writes that 'It was not the fact that extenuating circumstances can void obligations that drove philosophers to the naturalistic fallacy fallacy; it was rather a theory of language, as we shall see later on.' So the fallacy named is the accusers', and it consists in holding the gulf between is and ought to be unbridgeable. James C. Anderson of Syracuse University answered in Analysis ten years later with 'A Note on Searle's naturalistic fallacy fallacy', pages 139 to 141 of volume 34, which was not obtained here. Searle reworked the argument as chapter 8 of Speech Acts in 1969, and that book is lending-restricted at the Internet Archive, so this entry does not say whether the phrase recurs in it.

evidence: The record is philosophical on one side and a journal exchange in psychology on the other. Searle's own diagnosis is the interesting half, because it says why he thought the charge was being made wrongly rather than that it was. The inclination to accept a rigid distinction between is and ought, he writes, rests on a certain picture of the way words relate to the world, which he calls the classical empiricist picture and finds attractive himself. His complaint is that the picture cannot tell two kinds of statement apart. Statements containing words such as 'married', 'promise', 'home run' and 'five dollars' state facts whose existence presupposes an institution. Take away the institution of money and all a man has is a rectangular bit of paper with green ink on it; without baseball he only hits a sphere with a stick. Searle calls these institutional facts and contrasts them with brute facts, crediting Anscombe's 'Brute Facts' in Analysis in 1958 for the distinction, and he says the classical picture fails to account for the difference between the two. The institutions in question are systems of constitutive rules, which do not regulate an antecedently existing activity but define it, as the rules of chess do. Obligations, commitments, rights and responsibilities are institutionalised in the same way. The derivation itself, from a man uttering the words of a promise to his owing five dollars, is set out at entry 435, along with the replies it drew. What belongs here is the shape of Searle's move: he does not deny that people slide from is to ought, he denies that the slide is what his own five steps are doing. The psychological case is a 2011 exchange in Behavioral and Brain Sciences and it can be read in the two abstracts. Shira Elqayam and Jonathan St. B. T. Evans argued that normativism, the idea that human thinking reflects a normative system against which it should be measured and judged, 'invites the controversial "is-ought" inference, much contested in the philosophical literature'. They named two research programmes as committing it, Oaksford and Chater's rational analysis and Stanovich and West's individual differences approach, on the ground that equating norm and competence supports normative 'ought' theories with empirical 'is' evidence. Mike Oaksford and Nick Chater replied in the same issue under the title 'The "is-ought fallacy" fallacy'. Their abstract grants the premise and denies the application: 'Mere facts about how the world is cannot determine how we ought to think or behave... But this presumed application of the "is-ought" fallacy is itself fallacious. Rational analysis seeks to explain how people do reason, for example in laboratory experiments, not how they ought to reason. Thus, no ought is derived from an is.' That is the counter-charge in its clearest published form: not a defence of deriving ought from is, but a denial that any such derivation was made. Evans and Elqayam's response to the whole issue reports 29 commentators from philosophy and cognitive science as well as psychology, calls their views mixed, and says many defended a position the authors call soft normativism. The phrase has also been used as a settled term of art. Jan Wawrzyniak's 2006 article in Investigationes Linguisticae abbreviates it to NFF and argues that Searle took the fallacy to be linguistic in nature, citing pages 132 to 136 of Speech Acts, a reading this entry reports rather than adopts.

replication.headline: No study was found that counts how often the charge is misapplied, or that tests whether hearing it moves anyone's belief.
replication.detail: The search looked in four places. Crossref by title and by bibliographic query for the phrase and its variants returns the Anderson note of 1974, the Oaksford and Chater commentary of 2011, and otherwise the chapters of Sinclair's 2018 Cambridge volume on the naturalistic fallacy. OpenAlex's free-text search for the exact phrase returns 14 works, of which the two Anderson records are the only ones carrying it in a title. Europe PMC holds no record at all for the phrase, and its 15 records for 'is-ought fallacy' are commentary and opinion in bioethics, medical education and the psychology of reasoning. General web search surfaced fallacy dictionaries and no study. So the measured version of this page does not exist, and what does exist is adjacent in two directions. Sideways, entry 513 gives the pragma-dialectical figures for how ordinary arguers rate 24 types of fallacious move, in which this one does not appear. Downwards, the inference the charge is aimed at has been measured. Elqayam, Wilkinson, Thompson, Over and Evans ran two online experiments through CrowdFlower on what they call deontic introduction, the tendency to infer normative conclusions from descriptive premises. Experiment 1 recruited 116 and analysed 95 after exclusions; Experiment 2 recruited 235 and analysed 188. They report a selective defeasibility pattern, in which manipulations that suppressed deontic introduction also suppressed utilitarian moral judgement while leaving deontological judgement little affected. That is a study of people drawing the inference, by the authors who charged a field with committing it, and it tests nothing about the charge. Entry 435 carries the other measured line, Tworek and Cimpian's five studies and the one independent replication of them.

limits: Most of the primary material here was not obtained. Anderson's note is closed at Oxford and at JSTOR, Unpaywall reports no open location, and its two DOIs were verified at Crossref for author, journal, volume, issue, pages and date. Nothing is said above about what it argues. Speech Acts is lending-restricted at the Internet Archive, whose text file for the 1969 Cambridge printing returned an item-not-available page on two attempts, so Wawrzyniak's page references into it could not be checked. Both Behavioral and Brain Sciences items are behind a paywall and are quoted here from their abstracts on the publisher's landing pages, with the Oaksford and Chater abstract read a second time in Birkbeck's repository record; no figure from either article appears above, and the arguments in their bodies were not seen. Alex Walter's 'The Anti-Naturalistic Fallacy: Evolutionary Moral Psychology and the Insistence of Brute Facts' was located and verified at Crossref, and the publisher returned 403 to three attempts, so this page does not describe it. Whether Searle's derivation works is a separate question this entry does not take on, and entry 435 names Judith Jarvis Thomson and James Thomson's reply of the same year. No history of the phrase was found, so its use before 1964 is unknown here rather than absent. Wawrzyniak's article is a philosophy of language paper in a linguistics journal and is used only as a dated instance of the term in later use.
misreadings: The counter-charge is not a defence of the original argument. Showing that a fallacy label was misapplied leaves the argument exactly where it stood, to be judged on its own, which is the point entry 513 makes about the general case. It is also not the moralistic fallacy of entry 517, which runs from ought to is and is a different move by a different party. The second error is to hear Searle as denying that anyone ever slides from is to ought. His claim is about a class of derivations that pass through institutional facts, and his sentence naming the fallacy is a remark about what drove philosophers to the general prohibition. A third error is to expect the charge and the counter-charge to be about Moore. They are not. The name 'naturalistic fallacy' as used in these disputes means the is-ought prohibition, and entry 432 shows in Moore's own text that his fallacy is a claim about defining 'good', which he brought against metaphysical ethics as readily as against naturalism. A reader who arrives from Principia Ethica will find both sides arguing about something Moore did not say. Last, the Behavioral and Brain Sciences exchange is often described as a dispute about whether people reason well. It is a dispute about what a psychological theory is for. Elqayam and Evans argue that normative standards should be kept out of descriptive theory, Oaksford and Chater answer that rational analysis was descriptive all along, and this page adjudicates neither.

sources.text: Searle, J. R. (1964). How to Derive 'Ought' From 'Is'. The Philosophical Review, 73(1), 43-58. Read in full as a scan of the JSTOR copy, downloaded twice with identical checksums. The source for the coinage at page 48, for the sentence quoted from it, and for the classical picture, brute and institutional facts, and constitutive rules.

Anderson, J. C. (1974). A Note on Searle's naturalistic fallacy fallacy. Analysis, 34(4), 139-141. Not obtained. The record was verified at Crossref under this DOI and under the JSTOR duplicate 10.2307/3328017, and the Oxford landing page shows no abstract and offers the article as a PDF behind payment. Cited as the reply that exists.

Elqayam, S., & Evans, J. St. B. T. (2011). Subtracting 'ought' from 'is': Descriptivism versus normativism in the study of human thinking. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 34(5), 233-248. Closed at the publisher. Every phrase quoted from it was read from the abstract in the raw HTML of the publisher's page.

Oaksford, M., & Chater, N. (2011). The 'is-ought fallacy' fallacy. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 34(5), 262-263. Closed at the publisher. The abstract quoted above was read in the raw HTML of the publisher's page and again in Birkbeck's repository record, which reproduces it and states that the full text is not held there.
Oaksford, M., & Chater, N. (2011). The 'is-ought fallacy' fallacy. Birkbeck Institutional Research Online, eprint 4345. The second copy of the abstract, used to confirm the wording quoted here.

Evans, J. St. B. T., & Elqayam, S. (2011). Towards a descriptivist psychology of reasoning and decision making. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 34(5), 275-290. Closed at the publisher; the count of 29 commentators, the description of their views as mixed and the term soft normativism come from the abstract on the publisher's page.

Elqayam, S., Wilkinson, M. R., Thompson, V. A., Over, D. E., & Evans, J. St. B. T. (2017). Utilitarian Moral Judgment Exclusively Coheres with Inference from Is to Ought. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1042. Read as the full-text XML at Europe PMC, PMC5480028. The source for deontic introduction, the two CrowdFlower samples and the selective defeasibility pattern.

Wawrzyniak, J. (2006). The Logical Discipline of Normative Argumentation. Investigationes Linguisticae, 13, 196-206. Read in full as the journal PDF. Cited for its use of the phrase as a term of art, abbreviated NFF, and for its reading of Searle, which is reported rather than adopted.

Walter, A. (2006). The Anti-Naturalistic Fallacy: Evolutionary Moral Psychology and the Insistence of Brute Facts. Evolutionary Psychology, 4(1). Verified at Crossref and listed as open access by Unpaywall, and the publisher returned 403 on three attempts. Named as a neighbouring counter-charge that was not obtained, and nothing on this page rests on it.
